full_text:
An extreme heat warning remains in effect in San Diego County until at least 8 p.m. Thursday, as strong high pressure combined with offshore Santa Ana winds has triggered an unseasonably dangerous autumn heat wave.
Atmospheric conditions are driving temperatures 15 to 25 degrees above seasonal averages west of the mountains, with overnight lows remaining elevated in the 70s. Alongside the heat, meteorologists warn of an elevated fire weather danger fueled by weak to moderate easterly winds gusting between 20 to 35 mph, paired with exceptionally low relative humidity.
Beaches and coastal areas are experiencing an unusual heat wave as well, as offshore winds limit the normal cooling influence of the Pacific Ocean.

Daytime highs along the coast will spike into the mid-80s to mid-90s this week. High-exposure zones, including south-county locations and coastal mesas, are projected to approach 100 degrees before a gradual easing trend pulls temperatures back into the upper 80s by mid-week, according to the National Weather Service.
Triple-digit heat will remain persistent across inland valleys through Tuesday, with high temperatures ranging from 98 to 104. A slow downward trend is forecast to begin on Wednesday, lowering daytime highs back into the upper 80s and low 90s by Friday, the NWS said.
Higher elevations will be breezy and warm, with temperatures lingering in the mid-80s, which is slightly above the seasonal average, according to forecasters. Coastal mountain slopes face the highest fire risk due to localized easterly wind gusts reaching up to 35 to 40 mph.
Desert areas will get intense, dry heat throughout the week. High temperatures are forecast to range between 101 and 110, with peak thermal intensity expected during the middle to latter half of the week.
Residents were advised to limit strenuous outdoor physical activity, increase fluid intake, and ensure that children and pets are never left unattended in parked vehicles.
California power providers are also urging customers to conserve electricity whenever possible this week to help avoid outages.

With conditions becoming favourable for winds to gradually shift from westerlies to easterlies, thunderstorms are likely across most parts of the State over the next few days, accompanied by rumbling skies.
According to a weather bulletin issued by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Monday, an upper-air cyclonic circulation lies over North Interior Karnataka and the neighbourhood at 0.9 km above mean sea level. A trough extends from the Comorin area to the cyclonic circulation over North Interior Karnataka, passing across Tamil Nadu and South Interior Karnataka.
Under the influence of these weather systems, thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds reaching 30-50 kmph are very likely over parts of Keralam until October 9. A yellow alert has been issued for Idukki, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Palakkad, Malappuram, Kozhikode and Wayanad on Tuesday, warning of isolated heavy rainfall.
Meanwhile, the maximum temperature rose appreciably in Kozhikode and Kollam districts, with no significant change recorded elsewhere in Keralam during the 24 hours ending at 8.30 a.m. on Monday. Kozhikode and Punalur recorded the highest maximum temperature of 36.2°C, while Punalur recorded the lowest minimum temperature of 22.2°C.

Bay Area heat advisory extended through Thursday
A heat advisory remains in effect through 10 p.m. Thursday for much of the interior Bay Area and Central Coast.
Much of the Bay Area is facing hot weather through Thursday, with moderate to major heat risks expected across inland communities, the National Weather Service said Monday.
The hottest areas will be inland valleys, where temperatures are expected to reach the mid-80s to low 100s. The forecast calls for highs around 100 degrees in Concord and Livermore, 96 in Napa and Santa Rosa, and 93 in San Jose on Monday.
A heat advisory remains in effect through 10 p.m. Thursday for much of the interior Bay Area and Central Coast. The weather service warned that the heat can affect people without adequate cooling or hydration and advised residents to move outdoor activities to cooler parts of the day and never leave people or pets unattended in vehicles.
The heat will also raise fire danger in higher terrain through Thursday. Major HeatRisk is expected to remain widespread in parts of the East Bay through Tuesday and across the Santa Clara Valley through Wednesday.
Meanwhile, coastal flooding and beach hazards are expected to become a concern beginning Wednesday as high tides push water farther inland along some coastal and bayshore areas. The risks are expected to continue through Sunday.
Coastal flooding could affect low-lying roads, parks and trails, while beachgoers should watch for rip currents and sneaker waves.
